analysis.one_liner: Forces credit bureaus to fix disputed credit report errors and blocks deceptive credit-score subscription sales.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on June 24, 2021, drew zero cosponsors, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would overhaul how credit reporting agencies handle mistakes on credit reports. It would require a real investigation of disputes with trained staff, give consumers a free appeal if an error survives the first review, make lenders and debt collectors keep records backing up what they report, and explicitly allow courts to order agencies to stop unlawful practices. It would also ban the 'free' credit-score services that quietly auto-renew into paid subscriptions — a practice the three major bureaus were fined for — and require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules to make credit reports more accurate.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday consumers — especially the millions with errors on their reports that affect their ability to get a job, an apartment, a mortgage, or a credit card at fair rates. The bill's findings cite an FTC study in which 26% of participants found a potentially material error on their report, and where half of disputants gave up trying to fix errors.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a free, formal appeal process when a credit bureau's first review of a disputed item fails, handled by separate trained staff who cannot be paid or promoted based on how fast they process appeals [S3].

Requires bureaus to conduct an independent reinvestigation of disputes, pass along all of the consumer's supporting documents to the data provider, and stops bureaus and furnishers from dismissing repeat disputes as frivolous [S3].

Requires lenders, debt collectors, and other data furnishers to keep records substantiating what they report for as long as the information can appear on a report, and to notify consumers before reporting negative information [S3].

Bans automatic renewals for promotional credit reporting and credit scoring products and bars misleading marketing of credit scores — practices for which Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion were fined and ordered to pay restitution in 2017 [S3].

Gives consumers an explicit right to injunctive relief, so courts can order bureaus to fix unlawful practices rather than treating settlements as a cost of doing business, and requires accessible dispute information in multiple languages and formats [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three nationwide credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) and their credit monitoring and score subscription businesses, plus lenders, debt collectors, and other companies that furnish data and would bear record-keeping and investigation costs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on bureaus and furnishers, and the bill requires dispute and appeals staff to be located in the United States and forbids staffing decisions tied to processing speed — real operating costs that some argue could be passed on through credit product pricing [S3].

The bill prescribes detailed procedures rather than leaving standards to regulators, and its own findings acknowledge the bureaus were already under consent orders requiring similar marketing and dispute reforms, raising the question of how much was duplicative of existing enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a well-documented problem: credit report errors that people struggle for months to fix, with consequences for jobs, housing, and credit. The cost is compliance burden on a small number of large companies whose record on accuracy and marketing is documented in the bill's own findings — fines, consent orders, and quota systems for dispute handling. The main weakness is design, not merit: it layered detailed statutory procedures on top of enforcement that was already underway, and it went nowhere, so the tradeoff was never tested in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alma Adams introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the Congress [S4].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nationwide credit bureaus and the companies that furnish data to them keep the existing dispute system, including subscription products that convert into paid auto-renewals, untouched by this bill. Consumers with report errors gained nothing because it never came to a vote.

for.name: Rep. Alma S. Adams
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, laying out findings that credit bureaus use quota systems for dispute handling and that roughly a quarter of consumers find material errors on their reports.

sides.party_line_note: No committee action, no floor vote, and no cosponsors of either party ever materialized, so no partisan pattern was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The bill would force them to independently reinvestigate disputes, offer appeals, register with the CFPB, and stop the 'free' trial products that auto-convert to paid subscriptions — the same practices that drew 2017 fines and restitution orders documented in the bill's findings. Their interest in the existing system runs against consumers who bear the cost of errors.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and credit score subscription sellers
industries.note: The bill bans automatic renewals for promotional credit products and deceptive marketing of scores, cutting into a revenue stream built on consumers' confusion and fear about their own credit data.

industries.industry: Lenders, debt collectors, and other data furnishers
industries.note: They would have to keep substantiating records for as long as data stays on reports, investigate disputes independently with adequate staff, and give advance notice before reporting negative information — costs of accuracy they currently do not carry.
